docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK®
docs.text: This section details the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (MITRE ATT&CK®). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The MITRE ATT&CK® framework is arguably the industry standard for modeling traditional enterprise cyber threats. It provides a comprehensive matrix that classifies offensive actions taken by threat actors across various domains, such as Enterprise IT, Mobile, and Industrial Control Systems (ICS).

docs.title: Tactics
docs.text: A Tactic represents the “why” or the tactical objective of an adversary. It represents the reason for performing an action. Examples include Initial Access, Execution, and Privilege Escalation.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: A Technique represents “how” an adversary achieves a tactical goal. For instance, achieving the tactic of Initial Access might involve the technique of Phishing or Exploiting Public-Facing Applications. Techniques are often further divided into Sub-techniques for more granular descriptions of attacker behavior.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text: Mitigations are defensive concepts or mechanisms used to prevent or detect the execution of a technique.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams rely on the MITRE ATT&CK matrix as the primary operational framework for threat emulation and detection engineering. Instead of conducting uncoordinated penetration testing, the Red Team designs exercises around specific adversary techniques—such as exploiting public-facing applications or abusing command interpreters—while the Blue Team inspects detection telemetry in real time.

This collaborative dynamic allows engineers to identify and close visibility gaps across the enterprise. When the Red Team executes a technique, Blue observers verify whether endpoint sensors and security information and event management (SIEM) systems generate actionable alerts. The joint team tracks assessment outcomes across the matrix to establish a measurable detection scorecard: classifying each technique as blocked by preventative controls, detected through logged telemetry, or unmonitored. Blue engineers then author targeted detection rules, and the Red Team re-executes the procedure to validate alert fidelity.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: To map the concepts of MITRE ATT&CK® to the SCF C|P-RMM framework, one must align how each framework views the attacker versus the defense.

docs.title: 1. Tactics and Techniques Map vs. Threats
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat defines the “person or thing likely to cause damage.” MITRE ATT&CK® is essentially a detailed catalog of those sources of damage.

Tactics (the adversarial goal) and Techniques (the specific execution) represent the granular aspects of the Threat. When a malicious actor executes a Technique against a system, that is the literal materialization of the Threat in the SCF framework.

docs.title: 2. Mitigations vs. Controls
docs.text: Mitigations describe the precise security Controls needed to stop an attack.

docs.title: 3. The Realization of Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is created when a Threat exploits a Vulnerability.

When an adversary successfully executes a specific Technique because the system lacks the corresponding Controls (Mitigations were not implemented), the resulting damage is the Risk.

The MITRE ATT&CK® Tactic named Impact (TA0040) directly represents the realization of the Risk in SCF C|P-RMM.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text: MITRE ATT&CK® is heavily tailored toward generic endpoints, networks, and cloud infrastructure. When developing Large Language Model (LLM) applications or Agentic workflows, conventional tactics like lateral movement through active directory or exploiting OS-level vulnerabilities often do not capture the unique cognitive and application-level manipulations used against GenAI systems. Therefore, MITRE ATT&CK® must be used in conjunction with GenAI-focused frameworks such as MITRE ATLAS™ and OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications to provide a comprehensive view of GenAI threats.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] “MITRE ATT&CK.” https://attack.mitre.org/.

docs.title: MITRE CAPEC™
docs.text: This section details MITRE Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification (MITRE CAPEC™). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: MITRE CAPEC™ is a comprehensive catalogue of known attack patterns employed by adversaries to exploit known weaknesses. Attack patterns describe the common mechanisms, approaches, and methods adversaries use to compromise a system.

docs.title: Hierarchical Relationships
docs.text: Attack patterns are organized hierarchically. At the highest abstraction level, Categories group patterns sharing common characteristics. These cascade down into abstract Meta patterns, and finally into highly specific Standard and Detailed patterns focused on a particular execution methodology.

docs.title: Anatomy of an Attack Pattern
docs.text: When examining a specific attack pattern—such as Identity Spoofing (CAPEC-151)—the framework provides a structured decomposition of the adversary’s approach. Each entry specifies execution prerequisites, required attacker resources, and typical likelihood ratings alongside operational impact consequences. Direct mappings connect the pattern to underlying software flaws in MITRE CWE™ and specify actionable defensive mitigations.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use MITRE CAPEC to deconstruct attack patterns into granular execution stages that can be tested and defended incrementally. Because CAPEC documents the specific prerequisites, resource requirements, and step-by-step methodologies used by adversaries, the Red Team can construct precise, reproducible test cases rather than relying on ad-hoc exploit payloads.

During Purple Team engagements, Blue engineers use CAPEC’s attack flow breakdowns to position inspection points across each phase of an attack. When the Red Team executes a multi-step pattern, the Blue Team evaluates whether intermediate filters—such as input validation gateways or authentication boundaries—detect the initial probing before exploitation completes. Retesting confirmed attack patterns ensures that defensive controls address the underlying behavioral pattern rather than an isolated signature.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: To map the concepts of MITRE CAPEC™ to the SCF C|P-RMM framework, one must align the methodology of an attack with the exploitation of a system’s defenses.

docs.title: 1. Attack Patterns vs. Threats
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk materializes when a Threat successfully exploits a Vulnerability (a control deficiency).

MITRE CAPEC™ essentially catalogs the methodologies and mechanisms of precisely how that exploitation occurs. An Attack Pattern describes the exact process a Threat actor uses to leverage a specific Vulnerability (which is often defined by a MITRE CWE™).

docs.title: 2. Mitigations as Controls
docs.text: Just as SCF C|P-RMM relies on Controls to mitigate Vulnerabilities, each CAPEC Attack Pattern provides specific, actionable Mitigations. These recommendations correspond directly to the technical, operational, and architectural controls necessary to eliminate the control deficiency.

docs.title: 3. Consequences as Realized Risk
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk represents the quantifiable or qualitative damage that occurs when a threat exploits a control deficiency (Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact). The Consequences cataloged across CAPEC patterns—such as unauthorized data disclosure, system state corruption, or administrative privilege loss—represent the realization of that organizational risk.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text: Like most MITRE frameworks, MITRE CAPEC™ was primarily developed with traditional enterprise software, web applications, and network infrastructure in mind. While it accurately maps broad concepts like “Injection” or “Data Manipulation,” it often lacks the specialized depth required to natively model highly nuanced GenAI and Large Language Model (LLM) vectors, such as complex semantic prompt injection or model jailbreaking. Consequently, while CAPEC remains an excellent conceptual resource for understanding fundamental attack mechanics, securing modern agentic applications necessitates using it in conjunction with GenAI-focused frameworks like MITRE ATLAS™ and OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] “CAPEC - Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification (CAPEC™).” https://capec.mitre.org/index.html.

docs.title: MITRE CWE™
docs.text: This section details MITRE Common Weakness Enumeration (MITRE CWE™). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The MITRE CWE™ is a community-developed list of common software and hardware weakness types. A “weakness” is a condition in a software, firmware, hardware, or service component that, under certain circumstances, could contribute to the introduction of vulnerabilities.

A 2025 CWE Top 25 list has been published by MITRE, providing a very useful view of the most common and dangerous weaknesses, as of 2025.

docs.title: Weaknesses vs. Vulnerabilities
docs.text: In the MITRE CWE™ framework, a Weakness is an underlying flaw (e.g., inadequate input validation), while a Vulnerability is a specific occurrence of that weakness in a particular product (often tracked as a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVE).

docs.title: Hierarchical Structure
docs.text: MITRE CWE™ weaknesses are organized hierarchically. Pillars represent the most abstract weaknesses, which are broken down into Classes, then into Base level weaknesses, and finally into specific Variants. For example, the abstract concept of Improper Neutralization cascades down into granular variants like SQL Injection or Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use MITRE CWE to anchor security testing in root-cause flaw validation rather than superficial symptom mitigation. During joint assessments, the Red Team designs targeted exploit scenarios against specific weakness classifications—such as deserialization flaws (CWE-502) or improper input validation (CWE-20)—while the Blue Team audits static application security testing (SAST) rule coverage and runtime application defenses.

This collaboration ensures that engineering fixes eliminate the foundational software defect. When the Red Team successfully exploits a weakness, developers often deploy simple string filters that an attacker can easily bypass. In a Purple Team exercise, the Blue Team verifies that remediation addresses the underlying CWE class through structural controls, such as parameterized queries, strict schema validation, or safe serialization formats. The Red Team then re-tests the modified code path to verify that the entire weakness category has been neutralized.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: To map the concepts of MITRE CWE™ to the SCF C|P-RMM framework, one must align how each framework views systemic flaws and defensive gaps.

docs.title: 1. Weaknesses Map to Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is strictly defined as a Control Deficiency (a missing, ineffective, or failing defense).

The MITRE CWE™ provides a specific, standardized vocabulary to describe these very Control Deficiencies at a technical level. Therefore, instances of a CWE (a Weakness) represent the underlying technical flaws that directly constitute a Vulnerability in the SCF framework.

docs.title: 2. The Role in Realizing Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the result of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability.

While frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK® catalog the Threats (the “who” and “how” of the attack), MITRE CWE™ catalogs the Vulnerabilities (the gaps being exploited). Without the presence of a CWE (Weakness/Vulnerability), the Threat cannot successfully materialize into actual Risk.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text: The MITRE CWE™ is incredibly comprehensive and serves as the taxonomic foundation for many other security frameworks, including standard application security scanners. However, because it originated in traditional software engineering, it often approaches GenAI weaknesses abstractly. For instance, Prompt Injection is typically mapped to the broader concept of Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code (CWE-95), which fails to articulate the nuanced, semantic nature of LLM manipulation.

docs.text: [1] “CWE - Common Weakness Enumeration.” https://cwe.mitre.org/.

docs.title: NIST AI 100-2 E2023
docs.text: This section details the National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication AI 100-2e2023: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2 E2023). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Published in January 2024 as part of the NIST Trustworthy and Responsible AI series, NIST AI 100-2 E2023 establishes a foundational taxonomy and terminology for Adversarial Machine Learning (AML). The publication surveys modern adversarial research, establishing a formal conceptual hierarchy that covers predictive algorithms, deep neural networks, and generative language models.

Rather than cataloging isolated software bugs, the publication organizes adversarial machine learning across three fundamental dimensions: attacker goals, attacker capabilities, and lifecycle stages.

docs.title: 1. Attacker Goals and Objectives
docs.text:
NIST categorizes adversarial objectives into four primary security properties:

  • Integrity Violations: The adversary forces the model to produce incorrect predictions chosen by the attacker (targeted) or arbitrary erroneous outputs (untargeted), while preserving normal performance on benign inputs to avoid detection.
  • Availability Violations: The adversary degrades overall model utility or throughput. In generative architectures, this includes computational sponge attacks that maximize token generation latency, exhausting server GPU memory.
  • Confidentiality Violations: The adversary extracts proprietary information about model parameters, architecture, or internal latent representations (model stealing and model extraction).
  • Privacy Violations: The adversary infers whether specific sensitive records were included in the training dataset (membership inference) or reconstructs private training data verbatim (data extraction).

docs.title: 2. Attacker Capabilities and Knowledge
docs.text:
NIST establishes three distinct threat actor profiles based on access levels:

  • White-Box: The attacker possesses complete knowledge of the target system, including model weights, network architecture, training loss functions, activation values, and gradient data.
  • Black-Box: The attacker interacts with the system exclusively through inference queries, observing only emitted text or probability distributions without internal visibility.
  • Gray-Box: The attacker holds partial knowledge, such as the pre-training dataset distribution or model family, but cannot inspect internal runtime states or fine-tuned parameter weights.

docs.title: 3. Lifecycle Attack Stages
docs.text:
Adversarial interventions target two operational phases of the machine learning lifecycle:

  • Training and Development Phase: Attacks manipulate data collection, data preparation, or model fine-tuning. This stage encompasses data poisoning, where attackers inject malicious records into training sets, and backdoor attacks, where models are trained to associate specific trigger tokens with malicious behaviors.
  • Testing and Inference Phase: Attacks occur after deployment. Attackers submit crafted inputs (adversarial examples or prompt injections) designed to evade filters, trigger backdoors, or extract private information without altering model weights.

docs.title: Generative AI and Large Language Model Threat Taxonomy
docs.text:
Section 3 of the report provides a detailed classification of threats specific to generative models:

Section Attack Classification Threat Mechanism Typical Impact Section 3.1 Data Poisoning in Fine-Tuning Adversaries inject corrupted samples into pre-training corpora, instruction-tuning datasets, or reinforcement learning feedback loops. Compromised safety alignments, systematic political or corporate bias, and embedded latent backdoors. Section 3.2 AI Supply Chain and Deserialization Attackers publish compromised open-source models packaged in unsafe serialization formats like Python pickle files. Arbitrary code execution (RCE) on the host machine during model weight loading. Section 3.3.1 Direct Prompt Injection Attackers craft input prompts that overwrite system prompt constraints and bypass developer instructions. Unauthorized model behavior, jailbreaking, and execution of prohibited tasks. Section 3.3.2 Indirect Prompt Injection Adversarial instructions reside in untrusted third-party data sources (web pages, customer emails, documents) retrieved by the model. Data exfiltration, unauthorized API calls, and persistent semantic context manipulation. Section 3.4 Model Inversion and Training Extraction Attackers repeatedly query language models with structured prefixes to trigger memorized sequences. Reconstruction of proprietary source code, personal identifiable information (PII), and confidential training text.

docs.title: Mitigation Strategies in NIST AI 100-2
docs.text:
NIST identifies technical defenses across each lifecycle phase:

  • Training Defenses: Applying differential privacy algorithms during optimization, filtering web corpora for synthetic anomaly patterns, and computing cryptographic hashes over training checkpoints.
  • Format Hardening: Replacing unsafe execution-capable serialization formats with secure, read-only weight containers such as Safetensors.
  • Inference Defenses: Employing perplexity filters, output guardrails, and input sanitization to detect adversarial text sequences before they reach model context windows.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the NIST AI 100-2 E2023 taxonomy to calibrate adversarial testing across realistic attacker knowledge tiers and lifecycle stages. Because machine learning defenses vary substantially depending on what an adversary can access, the Red Team constructs exercises around specific threat profiles—testing black-box prompt extraction through public APIs or gray-box evasion against known foundation model families—while the Blue Team measures defensive efficacy.

This collaborative approach allows organizations to test both pre-deployment and runtime safeguards. During an exercise, the Red Team attempts to bypass input sanitizers and perplexity filters using obfuscated prompt injections, or probe fine-tuned models for training data leakage. The Blue Team evaluates whether runtime guardrails alert on adversarial token sequences and inspects output filtering policies to prevent sensitive text disclosure. Retesting against evolving attacker knowledge levels ensures that defensive controls remain effective even if internal model details leak.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: The formal taxonomy of NIST AI 100-2 E2023 maps directly to the SCF C|P-RMM model by distinguishing attacker mechanisms from system weaknesses and operational damages.

docs.title: 1. Adversary Profiles and Attacks as Threats
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat represents the external entity or action capable of inflicting damage. NIST’s knowledge tiers (White-Box, Gray-Box, Black-Box) model the threat actor’s capability, while specific attack techniques (Direct Prompt Injection, Data Poisoning, Sponge Attacks) represent the actionable threat vectors.

docs.title: 2. Architectural Gaps as Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is strictly defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or inadequately configured defensive mechanism).

NIST identifies these exact deficiencies: * Ingesting uncurated web scrape data without anomaly detection represents a data validation control deficiency. * Using unencrypted, unverified model serialization formats represents a software supply chain integrity deficiency. * Granting models direct access to external web content without strict delimiter separation represents an input boundary control deficiency.

docs.title: 3. Taxonomical Objectives as Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the consequence of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability (Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact).

NIST’s four attacker objectives correspond directly to organizational risk categories: * Integrity Risk: Flawed medical diagnoses, fraudulent automated approvals, or corrupted decision telemetry. * Confidentiality and Privacy Risk: Regulatory non-compliance and exposure of proprietary source code or confidential user records. * Availability Risk: Compute exhaustion, excessive cloud billing, and production application downtime.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
The primary contribution of NIST AI 100-2 E2023 is its scientific rigor. By anchoring modern generative AI vulnerabilities in established adversarial machine learning theory, the publication avoids the marketing hype that frequently distorts commercial security discussions. Its precise distinctions between attacker knowledge (White-Box vs. Black-Box) and attack lifecycles (training vs. inference) provide an objective foundation for enterprise risk assessment.

However, organizations applying NIST AI 100-2 must confront an essential technical constraint highlighted within the report:

Unlike classical cybersecurity vulnerabilities, where code patches can provide deterministic remediation, many generative AI attack surfaces lack complete theoretical defenses. In particular, prompt injection stems from the fundamental lack of mathematical separation between control instructions and data in natural language architectures. As NIST emphasizes, current defenses are heuristic and empirical, functioning to elevate attacker cost rather than providing guaranteed security boundaries. Security teams must therefore design defense-in-depth controls around the model rather than expecting model weights to defend themselves.

docs.title: NIST AI 100-2 E2025
docs.text: This section details the National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication AI 100-2e2025: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2 E2025). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Published in March 2025 as a finalized Special Publication, NIST AI 100-2 E2025 supersedes the earlier NIST AI 100-2 E2023 draft report. The publication establishes a formal, operationalized catalog for Adversarial Machine Learning (AML), transitioning exploratory research into an actionable baseline for enterprise threat modeling and risk management.

While the 2023 edition established foundational concepts, the 2025 edition introduces structural enhancements designed to integrate with automated vulnerability management pipelines and federal compliance frameworks.

docs.title: Key Structural Differences Between E2023 and E2025
docs.text:
The 2025 edition introduces four major structural evolutions over the 2023 release:

Assessment Dimension NIST AI 100-2 E2023 NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Taxonomy Taxonomy Indexing Referenced attacks through generic section numbers (such as Section 3.2 or Section 3.3). Establishes the formalized NISTAML machine-readable identification system (such as NISTAML.018:2025). Model Categorization Blended classical deep learning algorithms with emerging generative models across continuous sections. Explicitly bifurcates the threat landscape into Predictive AI (PredAI) and Generative AI (GenAI) architectures. Framework Integration Positioned primarily as an academic survey of literature and conceptual terminology. Directly maps adversarial attack classes and technical mitigations into the four core functions of the NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage). Mitigation Pragmatism Cataloged theoretical defense proposals from academic machine learning papers. Evaluates operational feasibility, explicitly documenting the absence of mathematically complete defenses for prompt injection.

docs.title: Predictive AI Versus Generative AI Threat Surfaces
docs.text:
NIST AI 100-2 E2025 establishes a clear operational boundary between two fundamentally distinct paradigms:

  • Predictive AI (PredAI): Systems designed for classification, regression, and detection tasks (such as fraud detection models or medical imaging classifiers). Attacks against PredAI center on mathematical optimization techniques, such as adding imperceptible adversarial noise (Fast Gradient Sign Method or Projected Gradient Descent) to shift feature vectors across decision boundaries, or poisoning training labels to degrade accuracy.
  • Generative AI (GenAI): Large language models and multimodal foundation architectures that generate dynamic, unstructured content. Attacks against GenAI exploit the semantic conflation between developer control instructions and user data, targeting conversational reasoning loops, retrieval context, and external tool execution.

docs.title: The NISTAML Taxonomy Catalog
docs.text:
The central innovation of the 2025 edition is the NISTAML numbering system. This schema provides unique, unambiguous identifiers that security operations centers, vulnerability registries, and automated scanners can reference directly:

NISTAML Identifier Attack Classification Target Modality Operational Mechanism NISTAML.010:2025 Data Poisoning PredAI & GenAI Injecting malicious samples or tainted instruction-tuning records into pre-training corpora or RLHF preference sets. NISTAML.015:2025 Indirect Prompt Injection GenAI Embedding hidden adversarial instructions in untrusted third-party documents, web pages, or email messages retrieved during inference. NISTAML.018:2025 Direct Prompt Injection GenAI Submitting adversarial conversational prefixes designed to bypass system prompt alignment and override developer guardrails. NISTAML.020:2025 Adversarial Evasion PredAI Adding calculated mathematical perturbations to inference inputs to force classification errors without human-perceptible distortion. NISTAML.025:2025 Supply Chain Deserialization PredAI & GenAI Distributing weaponized weight checkpoints using unsafe execution-capable formats like Python pickle that run arbitrary operating system commands upon loading. NISTAML.031:2025 Model Extraction PredAI & GenAI Submitting targeted query distributions to reconstruct proprietary model weights, decision boundaries, or tokenizer logic. NISTAML.033:2025 Membership Inference PredAI & GenAI Querying models to statistically verify whether specific confidential records were present in the training corpus. NISTAML.040:2025 Sponge Attacks GenAI Submitting crafted token sequences that trigger pathological computation cycles, exhausting host GPU memory and degrading throughput.

docs.title: Integration With NIST AI RMF 1.0
docs.text:
The 2025 standard bridges adversarial machine learning with broader enterprise governance by mapping specific technical mitigations directly to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1) core functions:

  1. Govern: Establishing policies that prohibit the unverified deployment of external open-source weights and mandating secure model registries.
  2. Map: Identifying whether application components interact with untrusted external text, untrusted third-party APIs, or unverified RAG vector stores.
  3. Measure: Benchmarking models against automated adversarial suites (evaluating empirical evasion rates, prompt extraction success rates, and token consumption bounds).
  4. Manage: Implementing defense-in-depth controls, including context delimiter isolation, input perplexity filtering, runtime guardrails, and cryptographic artifact signing.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the machine-readable NISTAML catalog from NIST AI 100-2 E2025 to index automated adversarial test suites and track defensive coverage. Because the 2025 specification separates Predictive AI from Generative AI, the Red Team tailors test playbooks to the exact model modality—executing mathematical evasion attacks (NISTAML.020:2025) against classification services or direct prompt injections (NISTAML.018:2025) against language models.

This standardized indexing connects offensive findings directly to enterprise risk metrics under the NIST AI RMF. When the Red Team executes an attack, Blue engineers verify whether detection rules and inference guardrails tag the event with the corresponding NISTAML identifier in security information and event management (SIEM) systems. This collaborative mapping validates the Measure and Manage functions of the AI risk framework, allowing teams to track mitigation progress across specific attack classes and verify that defenses withstand recurring exploitation attempts.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: The structured classification in NIST AI 100-2 E2025 maps into the SCF C|P-RMM model by connecting machine-readable attack codes with organizational control gaps and operational harm.

docs.title: 1. NISTAML Techniques as Threats
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat is the person or entity capable of causing damage. The NISTAML identifiers formally define the specific manifestations of that threat. An attacker executing an indirect prompt injection (NISTAML.015:2025) or a data poisoning campaign (NISTAML.010:2025) acts as the active threat agent.

docs.title: 2. Systemic Weaknesses as Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or inadequately configured defensive mechanism).

NIST AI 100-2 E2025 identifies the architectural control failures that allow NISTAML threats to succeed: * Ingesting user-supplied documents into an LLM context without delimiter enforcement represents an input boundary control deficiency. * Loading model checkpoints serialized with pickle instead of Safetensors represents a software supply chain integrity control deficiency. * Deploying unmonitored model endpoints without rate limiting represents an availability and resource governance deficiency.

docs.title: 3. Operational Outcomes as Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the business impact produced when a threat exploits a control deficiency (Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact).

NIST AI 100-2 E2025 aligns these impacts with core enterprise risk classes: * Integrity Risk: Flawed automated decision-making, compromised legal analysis, or biased diagnostic models resulting from prompt manipulation or data poisoning. * Confidentiality Risk: Unauthorized disclosure of internal system prompts, customer database entries, or proprietary source code through training data extraction (NISTAML.031:2025). * Availability Risk: Service outages, degraded response latency, and excessive cloud computing expenses caused by sponge attacks (NISTAML.040:2025).

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
The release of NIST AI 100-2 E2025 marks a major step forward for machine learning security by introducing the NISTAML identification taxonomy. In traditional cybersecurity, vulnerability management depends on shared catalogs like MITRE ATT&CK, CWE, and CVE. By assigning standardized codes to adversarial machine learning techniques, E2025 gives security operations teams a common language to index incident logs, track automated red team findings, and configure detection rules.

Furthermore, the explicit separation between Predictive AI and Generative AI resolves the confusion that plagued earlier frameworks, where traditional statistical attacks (like gradient-based evasion) were often conflated with natural language manipulation (like jailbreaking).

However, organizations adopting NIST AI 100-2 E2025 must manage a clear practical challenge:

Because the NISTAML identification schema was finalized in 2025, commercial security tooling, vulnerability databases, and existing regulatory audits are still transitioning away from the prose section numbers used in the 2023 edition. Security teams must maintain cross-reference mappings between legacy citations (such as Section 3.3.1) and current identifiers (NISTAML.018:2025) during this transitional phase.

docs.title: OWASP Artificial Intelligence Vulnerability Scoring System
docs.text: This section details the OWASP Artificial Intelligence Vulnerability Scoring System (OWASP AIVSS). [1], [2]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The OWASP Artificial Intelligence Vulnerability Scoring System is a specialized security framework engineered to evaluate vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous agent systems. While traditional vulnerability scoring standards like FIRST CVSS evaluate deterministic software flaws, OWASP AIVSS addresses the non-deterministic reasoning loops, tool-calling surfaces, and autonomous delegation capabilities inherent to agentic architectures.

OWASP AIVSS operates through a dual-methodology structure: 1. The OWASP AIVSS Version 0.8 Mathematical Framework: A quantitative calculation that takes a verified FIRST CVSS Base score as an empirical lower bound and amplifies it using ten operational risk factors, threat multipliers, and mitigation coefficients. 2. The OWASP AIVSS-SSVC Stakeholder Decision Model: A qualitative prioritization tree based on Carnegie Mellon University’s Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC), mapping exploitation likelihood, agent autonomy, and safety criticality to actionable remediation windows.

docs.title: The Need for Agent-Centric Vulnerability Scoring
docs.text:
When autonomous agents plan tasks, invoke external tools, generate code, and delegate sub-tasks to child agents, the security impact of a vulnerability extends beyond immediate host boundaries. A minor prompt injection or parameter parsing flaw can trigger persistent memory poisoning, arbitrary tool execution, recursive task decomposition, or financial resource exhaustion.

OWASP AIVSS resolves this challenge without abandoning enterprise risk practices. It retains compatibility with standard National Vulnerability Database (NVD) workflows by anchoring assessments in verified FIRST CVSS base vectors while systematically calculating the compounding risk uplift introduced by agent autonomy.

docs.title: The OWASP AIVSS Version 0.8 Mathematical Framework
Grounding in FIRST CVSS and Determining Score Headroom
docs.text:
OWASP AIVSS version 0.8 establishes its technical baseline using a verified FIRST CVSS Base score, drawn from either FIRST CVSS version 3.1 or version 4.0:

CVSS_Base ∈ [0.0, 10.0]

The framework calculates the available score headroom representing the theoretical maximum uplift contributed by agentic capabilities:

Headroom = 10.0 − CVSS_Base

If the baseline FIRST CVSS score is 8.7, the remaining headroom is 1.30. If the baseline score is 7.5, the available headroom is 2.50.

docs.title: The Ten Agentic Risk Amplification Factors
docs.text:
Assessors evaluate the vulnerable architecture against ten operational factors (F1 through F10), mapped directly to the OWASP Agentic AI Core Security Risks. Each factor is scored from 0.0 (no exposure) to 10.0 (unconstrained exposure):

  1. Factor F1 (Goal Hijacking): Evaluates whether an adversary can alter the primary objective, persona, or high-level trajectory of the agent.
  2. Factor F2 (Prompt Injection and Jailbreak): Measures exposure to direct system prompt extraction, jailbreaks, or indirect prompt injection via retrieved content.
  3. Factor F3 (Sensitive Information Disclosure): Assesses the risk of private context data, internal agent prompts, API keys, or operational telemetry leakage.
  4. Factor F4 (Supply Chain): Evaluates risks in third-party model weights, unsafe serialization formats, external dependencies, or unverified MCP server extensions.
  5. Factor F5 (Execution Engine Hijacking): Measures exposure of code execution runtimes, REPL interpreters, shell environments, or underlying containers.
  6. Factor F6 (Insecure Function Calling): Evaluates whether tools, APIs, and client methods validate arguments or enforce parameter boundaries.
  7. Factor F7 (Excessive Agency and Privilege Creep): Assesses whether the agent possesses unnecessary administrative privileges, unattended loops, or missing human approval gates.
  8. Factor F8 (Memory and State Poisoning): Measures vulnerability of long-term semantic memories, scratchpad logs, session state, or vector stores to persistent poisoning.
  9. Factor F9 (Multi-Agent Cascade): Evaluates whether corrupted agent decisions propagate downstream to compromise peer or child agents.
  10. Factor F10 (Denial of Wallet and Resource Exhaustion): Assesses vulnerability to infinite recursive agent loops, token flooding, API billing exhaustion, or system starvation.

The factors aggregate into a normalized Factor Sum on a 0.0 to 10.0 scale:

$$\text{Factor\_Sum} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{10} F_i}{10.0}$$

docs.title: Threat Multipliers and Mitigation Coefficients
docs.text:
The intermediate Agentic AI Risk Score (AARS) scales the headroom using the normalized factor ratio and the Threat Multiplier (ThM):

$$\text{AARS} = (10.0 - \text{CVSS\_Base}) \times \left(\frac{\text{Factor\_Sum}}{10.0}\right) \times \text{ThM}$$

The Threat Multiplier (ThM) captures adversary reach, capability, and exploit weaponization: - 0.50 – 0.80: Low capability; theoretical exploit requiring physical access or obscure internal configuration. - 0.90 – 1.10: Standard capability; remote network adversary using public tools or standard payloads. - 1.20 – 1.50: Advanced persistent adversary; weaponized automated exploit chains or coordinated campaigns.

The Mitigation Factor (M) evaluates existing defensive guardrails and architectural controls: - 1.00: No mitigations present, or existing controls bypassed completely. - 0.80 – 0.95: Partial mitigations; heuristic prompt filters, basic token limits, or post-execution logging without blocking. - 0.50 – 0.75: Comprehensive mitigations; isolated microVM sandboxing, cryptographic tool call verification, read-only state boundaries, and strict human authorization gates.

The final OWASP AIVSS version 0.8 score calculates as:

OWASP AIVSS = min (10.0,RoundHalfUp((CVSS_Base+AARS)×M,1))

Numerical scores map to qualitative severity ratings: None (0.0), Low (0.1–3.9), Medium (4.0–6.9), High (7.0–8.9), and Critical (9.0–10.0).

docs.title: The OWASP AIVSS-SSVC Stakeholder Decision Model
docs.text: While OWASP AIVSS version 0.8 calculates a quantitative score, the OWASP AIVSS-SSVC framework establishes operational triage priority and remediation timelines.

docs.title: Agent Autonomy Levels and Exposure Multipliers
docs.text: OWASP AIVSS-SSVC evaluates the level of autonomy granted to the agent: - Advisor (1.0× Multiplier): The agent provides advice, drafts, or analysis; all state-changing actions require human execution. - Collaborator (2.0× Multiplier): The agent executes tasks in a co-piloted configuration; critical tool calls require human confirmation. - Delegator (4.0× Multiplier): The agent operates autonomously within bounded administrative scopes, notifying operators asynchronously. - Prime Mover (8.0× Multiplier): The agent operates with complete end-to-end autonomy, unmonitored agent loops, dynamic tool selection, and elevated execution rights.

docs.title: Safety Criticality and Blast Radius
docs.text: Safety criticality measures the operational and physical blast radius of the system: - Low (1.0× Multiplier): Internal developer testing, non-production experiments, or read-only summarization. - Medium (2.0× Multiplier): Departmental business automation, customer support, or localized data transformations. - High (3.0× Multiplier): Enterprise business operations, confidential customer data pipelines, or continuous deployment systems. - Critical (4.0× Multiplier): Safety-of-life systems, healthcare diagnostic pipelines, critical infrastructure, or root corporate authorization control.

docs.title: Decision Outcomes and Remediation Windows
docs.text:
The product of likelihood, autonomy, and criticality yields a composite Risk Score:

Risk Score = Likelihood × Autonomy Multiplier × Safety Criticality Multiplier

This score resolves into four stakeholder remediation decisions:

Calculated Risk Score SSVC Decision Remediation SLA Window Recommended Operational Action ** ≥ 16.0** (or Prime Mover with score  ≥ 8.0) Immediate 0 to 7 Days Emergency out-of-band hotfix; immediately disable agent tool execution or isolate runtime. 8.0 – 15.9 Out-of-Cycle 7 to 30 Days Prioritize remediation outside the normal sprint cycle; deploy temporary guardrails. 3.0 – 7.9 Attend 30 to 60 Days Remediate during the next scheduled maintenance or regular engineering cycle. ** < 3.0** Track 60 to 90+ Days Monitor vulnerability telemetry; remediate during routine system refactoring.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
In artificial intelligence security exercises, Purple Teaming relies on OWASP AIVSS to unite offensive operators and defensive engineers around non-deterministic risks. While classical CVSS misclassifies prompt injections as low or moderate severities due to the absence of operating system crashes, an autonomous agent with tool execution rights can suffer complete hijacking from the same flaw. Purple teams use OWASP AIVSS to bridge this gap: the Red Team tests prompt extraction and tool exploitation, while the Blue Team monitors model telemetry, semantic guardrail activations, and unexpected agent state transitions.

The framework informs collaborative remediation across multi-stage agentic exploit chains. When Red operators chain an indirect prompt injection from an untrusted data source into goal diversion (F1) and unauthorized database tool execution (F6), Blue engineers use the attack telemetry to insert execution boundaries, such as human confirmation gates and schema-restricted parameter validation. The mathematical headroom formula captures this compound risk uplift, demonstrating how an initial prompt weakness escalates into severe organizational exposure.

Environmental calibration occurs through empirical testing of the Mitigation Factor (M) and SSVC autonomy classifications. Software and model vendors publish base evaluations under unconstrained assumptions. In a Purple Team exercise, Blue implements defensive guardrails, such as ephemeral container sandboxes and cryptographic tool verification, while Red attempts to bypass them. If Red circumvents the defenses, M remains at 1.00; if Blue’s controls contain the attack, the formula scales down the score. Concurrently, both teams review the SSVC Autonomy tier to establish agreed-upon remediation windows. High-autonomy Prime Movers receive immediate containment protocols, whereas supervised Advisors follow standard update cycles.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: To map the OWASP Artificial Intelligence Vulnerability Scoring System to the SCF C|P-RMM framework, one must examine how agentic capabilities transform control deficiencies into realized risk.

docs.title: 1. Translating Agentic Flaws to Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is strictly defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or inadequately configured defensive mechanism).

OWASP AIVSS’s ten Risk Amplification Factors systematically categorize the specific Control Deficiencies unique to generative AI and autonomous agent implementations: - Missing tool parameter validation represents an input validation control deficiency (Factor F6). - Unbounded execution loop limits represent a resource management control deficiency (Factor F10). - Missing cryptographic identity verification between agents represents an authentication control deficiency (Factor F9). - Persistent state mutability without integrity checks represents a configuration integrity deficiency (Factor F8).

docs.title: 2. Operationalizing Risk Amplification
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the consequence of a Threat successfully exploiting a Vulnerability (Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact).

OWASP AIVSS operationalizes this definition for autonomous systems: - Classical FIRST CVSS Base scores measure the baseline technical vulnerability. - The Agentic AI Risk Score (AARS) mathematically models the compounded Risk realized when the vulnerability is exploited by an autonomous entity capable of secondary tool use, subagent delegation, and unmonitored execution. - The OWASP AIVSS-SSVC decision framework translates this realized risk into concrete governance outcomes, establishing enforceable remediation windows that reflect the true operational blast radius of the system.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
The OWASP Artificial Intelligence Vulnerability Scoring System provides an essential evolution in vulnerability management, addressing the blind spots that arise when classical scoring models encounter autonomous agent architectures. By establishing FIRST CVSS Base scores as an empirical floor rather than a ceiling, OWASP AIVSS ensures backwards compatibility with enterprise CVE infrastructure while accurately measuring the compounded exposure introduced by agent autonomy.

However, because OWASP AIVSS is an evolving standard, organizations must account for specific operational considerations. The rapid development of agentic architectures means the amplification factors must undergo regular review to reflect emerging interaction patterns.

Despite these ongoing refinements, OWASP AIVSS represents the most comprehensive, standardized framework available for quantifying and managing vulnerabilities in generative AI and autonomous agent systems.

docs.title: OWASP Top Ten Web Application Security Risks
docs.text: This section details the OWASP Top Ten Web Application Security Risks. [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The OWASP Top 10 is a standard awareness document for developers and web application security. It represents a broad consensus about the most critical security risks to web applications, updated periodically by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) community.

docs.title: Focus Areas
docs.text:
The framework categorizes vulnerabilities broadly to encompass overarching trends. In the latest edition, the list shifted towards root-cause categories:

  1. A01: Broken Access Control: Failures in enforcing user permissions and restrictions.
  2. A02: Cryptographic Failures: Inadequate protection of sensitive data in transit and at rest.
  3. A03: Injection: Flaws where untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command.
  4. A04: Insecure Design: Risks related to architectural and design flaws rather than implementation defects.
  5. A05: Security Misconfiguration: Insecure default settings, open cloud storage, or misconfigured HTTP headers.
  6. A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components: Exploiting systems with known vulnerable dependencies.
  7. A07: Identification and Authentication Failures: Weaknesses allowing attackers to compromise passwords or session tokens.
  8. A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures: Making assumptions related to software updates, critical data, and CI/CD pipelines.
  9. A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures: The inability to detect or respond to an active breach.
  10. A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): Flaws occurring when a web application fetches a remote resource without validating the user-supplied URL.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the OWASP Top 10 to establish the baseline verification scope for web applications, APIs, and modern frontends. Because web vulnerabilities frequently serve as the initial entry point for broader compromise, the Red Team executes targeted test cases against each category—such as probing for broken access control (A01), injecting malicious commands into backend parsers (A03), or exploiting server-side request forgery (A10)—while the Blue Team audits defensive filtering and telemetry.

This joint testing ensures that defensive layers actively detect and block common attack patterns. When the Red Team attempts to bypass authorization checks or exploit vulnerable dependencies (A06), Blue engineers inspect web application firewall (WAF) logs, API gateway policies, and application telemetry to confirm alert generation. The Purple Team documents whether each category is effectively blocked or monitored, implementing hardened configurations before repeating the exercise to confirm verified remediation.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: Mapping the OWASP Top 10 to the SCF C|P-RMM framework aligns common web flaws with systemic control deficiencies and organizational harm.

docs.title: 1. Web Exploits as Threats
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat represents the external person or action capable of inflicting harm. The adversarial acts described across the OWASP Top 10—such as automated credential stuffing, injection payloads, or manipulated HTTP request headers—represent active threat vectors targeting the application boundary.

docs.title: 2. Category Weaknesses as Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or misconfigured defense).

The OWASP Top 10 categories directly represent systemic control deficiencies: - Broken Access Control (A01) reflects missing or improperly enforced authorization controls. - Cryptographic Failures (A02) reflect inadequate data-in-transit or data-at-rest encryption controls. - Security Misconfiguration (A05) reflects missing baseline hardening or default credential management controls.

docs.title: 3. Operational Consequences as Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the consequence of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability (Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact).

The consequences resulting from OWASP Top 10 exploits—including corporate database leakage, compromised customer accounts, financial fraud, and host infrastructure takeover—constitute the realization of business risk.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text: The standard OWASP Top 10 remains essential because every web-based LLM application or Agentic interface is, ultimately, still a web application. However, it does not account for the probabilistic and non-deterministic nature of GenAI. While injection (A03) conceptually overlaps with Prompt Injection, the traditional mitigation strategies for SQLi or XSS (parameterization, strict escaping) are structurally incompatible with natural language LLM interfaces.

docs.text: [1] “OWASP Top Ten Web Application Security Risks OWASP Foundation.” https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/.

docs.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications
docs.text: This section details the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026. [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: While the standard OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications focuses on the risks inherent to interacting with language models, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 shifts the perspective to systems equipped with autonomy. An agentic application plans, makes decisions, and delegates tasks to external tools, APIs, or secondary agents in addition to generating text.

docs.title: The Emerging Agentic Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
These vulnerabilities highlight active, behavioral, and architectural risks:

  1. ASI01 — Agent Goal Hijack: Manipulating the agent’s objectives via malicious inputs, diverging its trajectory from the intended objective.
  2. ASI02 — Tool Misuse and Exploitation: Tricking the agent into leveraging its authorized toolset (e.g., executing scripts, querying databases) for unauthorized or malicious acts.
  3. ASI03 — Identity and Privilege Abuse: Exploiting the credentials and excessive permissions granted to an autonomous agent to perform unauthorized actions.
  4. ASI04 — Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities: Risks stemming from compromised external dependencies, third-party API dependencies, or malicious prompt templates the agent relies upon.
  5. ASI05 — Unexpected Code Execution (RCE): Leveraging the agent’s execution abilities to run malicious commands within the agent’s host environment.
  6. ASI06 — Memory and Context Poisoning: Injecting malicious payloads into an agent’s persistent memory, corrupting the information it uses to make long-term decisions.
  7. ASI07 — Insecure Inter-Agent Communication: Vulnerabilities exposing or manipulating the data transferred between multiple collaborating agents.
  8. ASI08 — Cascading Failures: A single node or decision failure causing a chain reaction of failures or malicious actions across a distributed multi-agent system.
  9. ASI09 — Human-Agent Trust Exploitation: Deceiving human operators into trusting the agent’s outputs, leading to the approval of risky actions or data disclosure.
  10. ASI10 — Rogue Agents: Loss of control or emergent unsafe behaviors causing the agent to act outside of its established guardrails or design.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications to evaluate the operational risks created by autonomous planning loops, tool execution capabilities, and inter-agent delegation. Because agentic architectures possess active execution rights across backend APIs and operating system environments, the Red Team designs exercises to test whether autonomous agents can be forced off their intended trajectory—such as executing goal hijacking (ASI01), manipulating tool invocations (ASI02), or poisoning persistent vector memory (ASI06)—while the Blue Team inspects runtime observability pipelines.

This collaborative approach allows organizations to establish defense-in-depth across the agent runtime. When the Red Team attempts to induce unauthorized tool actions or trigger unexpected code execution (ASI05), Blue engineers evaluate whether sandbox boundaries, cryptographic tool call verification, and human-in-the-loop approval gates successfully contain the behavior. The Purple Team tracks mitigation performance across each agentic category, implementing least-privilege credential scoping and schema-constrained tool parameters before retesting to verify that agent autonomy remains bounded.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: Mapping the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications to the SCF C|P-RMM framework connects agent autonomy risks with systemic control deficiencies and business consequences.

docs.title: 1. Agentic Exploits as Threats
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat represents the external entity or event capable of causing harm. In autonomous systems, threats manifest as malicious actors submitting adversarial goal-altering inputs, rogue peer agents transmitting corrupted coordination messages, or compromised third-party plugins in the agent supply chain.

docs.title: 2. Autonomous Flaws as Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is strictly defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or inadequately configured defensive mechanism).

The OWASP Agentic Top 10 categories directly reflect control deficiencies in system architecture: - Tool Misuse and Exploitation (ASI02) reflects absent parameter boundary enforcement and missing authorization checks on tool methods. - Identity and Privilege Abuse (ASI03) reflects excessive administrative privileges granted to the agent runtime. - Memory and Context Poisoning (ASI06) reflects missing integrity validation on persistent semantic stores and vector embeddings.

docs.title: 3. Systemic Breakdown as Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the consequence of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability (Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact).

When an adversary exploits an agentic control deficiency, the resulting impacts—such as fraudulent financial transactions executed via tools, host operating system compromise through unexpected code execution, or cascading multi-agent deadlocks—represent the realization of organizational risk.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text: The Agentic Top 10 is necessary because simply patching the vulnerabilities listed in OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications is insufficient for modern AI systems. This framework accurately portrays the dangers that lie in the agency given to the system. However, agentic tooling evolves rapidly, and this catalog may require frequent updates.

docs.text: [1] “OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026,” OWASP Gen AI Security Project. https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/.

docs.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
docs.text: This section details the OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications. [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications educates developers, designers, architects, managers, and organizations about the potential security risks when deploying and managing Large Language Models.

docs.title: The Top 10 Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
The list specifically highlights the novel attack surfaces introduced by deep learning architectures:

  1. LLM01: Prompt Injection: Crafting inputs that manipulate the LLM into circumventing security boundaries or executing unintended commands.
  2. LLM02: Insecure Output Handling: Blindly trusting the output generated by the LLM without adequate downstream validation, leading to issues like XSS or SSRF in the backend application.
  3. LLM03: Training Data Poisoning: Manipulating the data or fine-tuning processes to introduce vulnerabilities, biases, or backdoors into the underlying model.
  4. LLM04: Model Denial of Service: Causing resource exhaustion by interacting with the LLM in ways that require excessive computation or context window consumption.
  5. LLM05: Supply Chain Vulnerabilities: Compromises originating from third-party sets of training data, pre-trained models, or vulnerable plugin dependencies.
  6. LLM06: Sensitive Information Disclosure: The LLM inadvertently revealing confidential data, PII, or internal system details from its prompt structure or training data.
  7. LLM07: Insecure Plugin Design: Plugins that ingest untrusted inputs with insufficient access controls or validation before executing downstream processes.
  8. LLM08: Excessive Agency: Granting an LLM system a high degree of functionality, autonomy, or privileges without proper oversight or restrictions.
  9. LLM09: Overreliance: Users completely depending on LLM outputs without human oversight, leading to the propagation of hallucinations or misinformation.
  10. LLM10: Model Theft: Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of proprietary LLM models through physical theft, API extraction, or weight harvesting.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Models to establish a specialized test plan for generative AI applications. Because language models process unstructured natural language instructions alongside user data, the Red Team executes focused test scenarios across the catalog—such as crafting direct and indirect prompt injections (LLM01), testing whether generated text triggers downstream cross-site scripting (LLM02), or probing for excessive tool permissions (LLM08)—while the Blue Team measures defensive visibility.

During joint exercises, Blue engineers evaluate whether input guardrails, output sanitizers, and token rate limits detect and intercept adversarial interactions. If the Red Team demonstrates that an indirect prompt injection forces the model to emit an unvalidated SQL query or disclose confidential system instructions (LLM06), the Blue Team immediately reconfigures defensive boundaries. These remediations include enforcing strict output encoding on application parsers, restricting plugin privileges, and inserting human confirmation gates before state-changing tool executions. Retesting the scenario confirms whether the combined controls neutralize the attack path.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: Mapping the OWASP Top 10 for LLM to the SCF C|P-RMM framework translates language model vulnerabilities into systemic control deficiencies and organizational harm.

docs.title: 1. Adversarial Interactions as Threats
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat represents the external entity or event capable of causing harm. In the context of LLM applications, threats encompass external attackers submitting adversarial prompt injections, malicious insiders poisoning fine-tuning datasets, or unauthorized consumers extracting model weights.

docs.title: 2. Architectural Vulnerabilities as Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is strictly defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or inadequately configured defensive mechanism).

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM items identify specific control deficiencies in application design: - Insecure Output Handling (LLM02) reflects an absent output sanitization and encoding control. - Insecure Plugin Design (LLM07) reflects missing parameter validation and authentication controls on downstream tools. - Excessive Agency (LLM08) reflects a failure of least-privilege access control and missing human-in-the-loop authorization gates.

docs.title: 3. Exploit Consequences as Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the consequence of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability (Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact).

When an adversary exploits an LLM control deficiency, the resulting impacts—such as remote command execution on host servers, regulatory fines for leaked confidential training records, or service outages caused by model denial of service—represent the realization of business risk.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text: The OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications provides a critical bridge between traditional AppSec and AI engineering. However, it often blurs the boundary between concrete application vulnerabilities (e.g., Insecure Output Handling) and fundamental model limitations (e.g., Overreliance is more a user behavior risk than a technical exploit). Additionally, as applications move from single-turn chatbot interactions to autonomous multi-agent workflows, this list can sometimes feel too static to fully capture emergent behavioral risks.

docs.text: [1] “OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications OWASP Foundation.” https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/.

docs.title: SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: This section details the Secure Controls Framework — Cybersecurity & Data Privacy Risk Management Model (SCF C|P-RMM). [1] [2] The perspective provided by such framework is central to the book, as it clearly defines Threats versus Vulnerabilities and Risks.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The SCF C|P-RMM is part of a comprehensive Risk Management Ecosystem. This “meta-framework” unifies a diversity of controls from standards like NIST, ISO, and GDPR into a single cohesive practice. Its core principle is clear: Cybersecurity teams manage Controls, but business units own Risk. Rather than battling inevitable external threats, the framework focuses on aligning internal controls with the organization’s risk tolerance.

Figure 1 illustrates this Risk Management Ecosystem. It depicts Risk not as an isolated event, but as the calculated result of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability. This visual distinction is critical: Threats are inevitable, but Vulnerabilities are manageable. By strengthening controls, organizations break the chain before Risk is realized.

Figure 1: Risks vs Threats vs Vulnerabilities according to SCF C|P-RMM.

docs.title: Threat
docs.text: A Threat is defined by the SCF C|P-RMM as a person or thing likely to cause damage or danger. It represents the potential negative action or event whether natural (e.g., floods, earthquakes) or man-made (e.g., hackers, insiders) that could impact the organization. Threats are generally external to the control environment or inevitable forces that the organization must prepare for but cannot directly eliminate.

docs.title: Vulnerability
docs.text: A Vulnerability is associated with Control Deficiencies. It is a weakness or gap in the organization’s defenses where a Control is either missing, ineffective, or failing to function as expected. When a Threat materializes, it is the presence of a Vulnerability that allows the Threat to cause actual harm.

docs.title: Risk
docs.text: Risk is the situation where someone or something valued is exposed to danger, harm, or loss. It is the result of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability. In the SCF C|P-RMM model, risk is the business’s quantifiable or qualitative potential for loss.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teaming operationalizes the tripartite core of the SCF C|P-RMM framework. While cybersecurity theory divides operations into external threats and internal defenses, Purple Teaming unites the Red Team (which emulates active Threats) and the Blue Team (which identifies and manages Control Deficiencies) into a synchronized exercise. By simulating threat actor behaviors against targeted controls, the joint team verifies whether defensive mechanisms hold before an adversary can realize business Risk.

The framework provides Purple teams with a shared metric to evaluate control performance. When an offensive operator demonstrates that an attack succeeds, the team does not merely document an isolated compromise; it identifies the exact control failure—such as missing authentication or failing boundary inspection—that permitted the exploitation. The Blue Team can then reconfigure the deficient control or introduce compensating defenses, after which the Red Team immediately re-tests the vector. This iterative feedback loop transforms abstract risk management into an empirical, measurable validation of organizational resilience.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text: The “Threat Catalog,” as found in SCF C|P-RMM, is often seen as broad beyond the point of being useful. Listing “NT-13 Volcanoes” alongside “MT-2 Hacking” flattens threat prioritization. For most organizations, natural disasters are distinct from cybersecurity operations, yet they occupy space in the framework and require mental overhead to scope out. The noise obscures the signal of actual, probable threats.

docs.title: Adaptation for GenAI Security Purposes
docs.text: In the spirit of the above critique, Gurple takes the approach of building on top of the SCF C|P-RMM framework, by going one level deeper into the “Threat Catalog.” The Threats discussed in Gurple, will be, then, more specific and relevant to GenAI Security. This specialized approach is detailed in the Threats chapter.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Jailbreaking is a threat where an adversary crafts adversarial prompts to bypass the safety alignment, content moderation filters, and behavioral guardrails of a Large Language Model (LLM). Rather than targeting application permissions or host execution layers, jailbreaking exploits the model’s instruction-following nature to elicit prohibited, hazardous, or policy-violating outputs that the system was trained to refuse.

Adversaries achieve jailbreaks by exploiting the fundamental tension between helpfulness and safety in aligned models. Through techniques such as persona adoption, adversarial suffix optimization, linguistic ciphering, multi-turn escalation, and hypothetical context framing, the input forces the model’s objective of fulfilling user requests to override its refusal mechanisms.

Note

Refer to the note in the Prompt Injection section for the distinction between Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Prompt Injection is a threat where an attacker manipulates the inputs to alter the behavior of a GenAI system, often via user prompts, forms, or attached data. By disguising malicious inputs, an adversary can bypass guardrails and induce the AI to perform unauthorized actions, or execute arbitrary code.

Note

In Gurple, distinction is made between Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking.

The next section is dedicated to Jailbreaking, which is a subset of Prompt Injection. In this case, the goal is to abuse the model’s safety guardrails stack (e.g., RLHF, fine-tuning, AI Judges) to generate restricted content or behaviors.

To create a clear separation, the present section, named Prompt Injection, is restricted to attacks that bypass the security layers of the GenAI system (e.g. authentication, authorization, input / output validation).

One must also recognize that threats are not found in isolation in the wild, and that most real-world threats are chained attacks, where a hacker uses multiple techniques to achieve their goal. For example, a hacker may utilize a sequence of prompts that manipulate context to bypass the model’s safety guardrails stack while also concealing inputs that will trigger code execution. In such cases, the line between Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking becomes blurred.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Deserialization of untrusted data occurs when an application deserializes data from an untrusted source without sufficient validation. In the context of GenAI, this vulnerability can be exploited when the model processes serialized objects (e.g., JSON, pickle, joblib) [1] provided via prompts or attached data. Specifically for Exfiltration, the adversarial prompt is designed to coerce the system into reading sensitive data from the system’s environment or filesystem (e.g., API keys, user credentials) and transmitting it back as chat answers or logs that may be further exploited.

docs.title: Mechanism
docs.text:
Starting from a safe serialized object in the expected format, the attacker crafts a tampered object that evades deserialization controls. The payload is then injected into user input to the GenAI system (e.g., user prompts, forms, attached data).

Figure 1: Deserialization of Untrusted Data [2].

To result in Exfiltration, the payload is specifically engineered to output information from files (e.g., /etc/passwd, .env files), databases, or environment variables.

docs.title: Attack Entry Points
docs.text:
Exfiltration Through Deserialization attacks can be executed through any Entry Point where a serialized object could be passed on to the system, even if disguised as regular text or data, to be later deserialized.

  • The Front Door 🚪 — Network & Application Interfaces

    • Application Programming Interface (API) Endpoints

    • User Interface (UI)

    • Sensors

      Note: Nothing really prevents an attacker from writing a serialized object on a QR code, a sign, or a t-shirt and presenting it to a camera, or dictating it to a voice-activated assistant.

    • Observability Integration Interfaces

  • The Side Door 🚪 — Supply Chain

    Note: Exploitation of deserialization vulnerabilities in dependencies.

  • The Back Door 🚪 — Data Storage

  • The Hidden Door 🚪 — Event-Driven & Serverless Triggers

    • Indirect Sources
    • Agentic Tools
    • Model Context Protocol (MCP)
    • Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A)
    • Infrastructure Events

docs.title: System Impact
docs.text:
The vulnerability does not immediately disrupt service availability or corrupt the host runtime during deserialization. The deserialization vulnerability can be exploited to exfiltrate sensitive information from the system, but it does not directly impact the system’s functionality or performance.

Note, however, that the exfiltrated information can include keys to decode encrypted data, and may be used to exploit the system further.

docs.title: Business Impact
docs.text: Sensitive information is exfiltrated from the system, impacting Business Continuity. The exfiltrated information can include secrets to access other services (e.g. APIs, databases), user credentials, or other sensitive data.

docs.title: Financial Impact
docs.text: Attackers can gain access to financial data, such as credit card numbers, bank account numbers, or other sensitive records. They can also harvest resources across integrated services using the exfiltrated secrets.

docs.title: Legal Impact
docs.text: Data breaches expose the organization to civil litigation, customer breach-of-contract claims, and liability for downstream compromise.

docs.title: Operational Impact
docs.text: Remediation requires emergency downtime to revoke credentials, rotate infrastructure secrets, and inspect pipeline logs.

docs.title: Regulatory Impact
docs.text: Leaking unencrypted user data or personal identifiable information violates GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI DSS, leading to statutory fines and mandatory audits.

docs.title: Reputational Impact
docs.text: Public disclosure of sensitive data exfiltration damages brand credibility and erodes customer trust.

LangGrinch exploits the internal serialization mechanism of LangChain Core. The library uses a reserved key, "lc": 1, to distinguish serialized LangChain objects from regular dictionaries.

The vulnerability involves two stages:

  1. Injection: The dump() and dumps() functions failed to escape dictionaries containing the "lc": 1 key. An attacker can prompt the LLM to output a JSON object with this key (e.g., in a metadata field). When the application serializes this output (for logging or history), the malicious payload is stored as a valid serialized object.

  2. Deserialization: When the application later retrieves and deserializes this data using load() or loads(), it instantiates the object defined by the attacker instead of a simple dictionary.

Example:

from langchain_core.load import dumps, loads
import os

# Attacker injects secret structure into user-controlled data
attacker_dict = {
    "user_data": {
        "lc": 1,
        "type": "secret",
        "id": ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]
    }
}

serialized = dumps(attacker_dict)  # Bug: does NOT escape the 'lc' key

os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = "sk-secret-key-12345"
deserialized = loads(serialized, secrets_from_env=True)

print(deserialized["user_data"])  # "sk-secret-key-12345" - SECRET LEAKED!

Attack Vectors:

  • Secret Exfiltration (Default Behavior): Prior to the patch, the secrets_from_env parameter involved in deserialization was set to True by default. This allowed a serialized object to request the value of an environment variable.
    • Mechanism: The attacker defines an object with type: "secret" and points it to a target variable (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY).
    • Outcome: The deserializer reads the server’s environment variable and populates the object with the secret, effectively pulling it into the application’s memory scope where it can be leaked in logs or responses.
  • Blind Side-Channel Exfiltration: Attackers can trigger network requests during the object instantiation process (e.g., via the __init__ method of allowed classes).
    • Mechanism: Classes such as langchain_aws.ChatBedrockConverse were found to perform network validation on initialization. An attacker can craft a payload that instantiates this class, sets a custom endpoint_url to a server they control, and inserts a sensitive environment variable into the request headers.
    • Outcome: The server sends the secret directly to the attacker’s listener during the deserialization step, regardless of whether the object is displayed to the user.
  • Remote Code Execution (RCE): While more complex, RCE is possible if the attacker forces the instantiation of a PromptTemplate using Jinja2 templates. If the application logic subsequently renders this template, arbitrary Python code execution can be achieved.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Injection of Serialized Object: The attacker submits a prompt designed to coerce the LLM into returning a specially crafted JSON object (containing the "lc": 1 key) as part of its output, for example in additional_kwargs or metadata fields.

  2. Deserialization: The application subsequently reads and deserializes the LLM response by using a vulnerable library function (e.g., langchain-core’s load() or loads()).

  3. Exploitation: Upon deserialization, the malicious JSON is interpreted as a valid object definition. To exfiltrate secrets, the attacker targets the secrets_from_env mechanism, causing the library to read sensitive environment variables (like OPENAI_API_KEY) and populate the object with the secret value, which is then exposed.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The attacker successfully exfiltrates the target environment variable value(s) from the application.

GenAI systems frequently hallucinate plausible environment variable strings. Operators must validate captured values against live services to confirm authenticity.

docs.title: Prompting the Production Application

The attacker submits a malicious prompt directly to the production application. The prompt is designed to coerce the LLM into returning a specially crafted JSON object (containing the "lc": 1 key) as part of its output that will be passed to langchain-core’s load() or loads() functions:

{
    "user_data": {
        "lc": 1,
        "type": "secret",
        "id": ["SECRET"]
    }
}

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Libraries: Upgrade langchain-core to version >=1.2.5. These patched versions disable dangerous features like secrets_from_env by default and block Jinja2 templates.

  • Restrict Deserialization: Use the allowed_objects parameter in load() and loads() functions to explicitly whitelist safe classes and disallow arbitrary object instantiation.

  • Disable Secrets from Env: Explicitly set the configuration secrets_from_env=False in your application logic if not relying on defaults.

  • LLM Input/Output Validation: Validate all model input and output, including metadata and additional_kwargs, before deserialization.

  • GenAI System Output Validation: Implement rigorous validation for the AI system outputs, which includes the whole workflow, or chain. Ensure that outputs containing sensitive patterns, such as cryptographic hashes or API keys, are either blocked or appropriately redacted before being logged or displayed to users.

import re


class LlmIoValidator:
    """Validates LLM input and/or output strings for potential deserialization attacks.

    Uses pre-compiled regex patterns to check if the raw text contains
    signatures that could trigger deserialization vulnerabilities.
    """

    # Pre-compile the regex patterns for performance
    _SENSITIVE_PATTERNS = [
        re.compile(r'"lc"\s*:\s*1'),
        re.compile(r'"type"\s*:\s*"constructor"'),
        re.compile(r'"type"\s*:\s*"exec"'),
        re.compile(r'"type"\s*:\s*"secret"'),
        re.compile(r'__init__'),
        re.compile(r'langchain'),
        re.compile(r'Bedrock'),
        re.compile(r'"endpoint_url"'),
        # Add more patterns as needed
    ]

    @classmethod
    def validate(cls, text: str) -> bool:
        """Validates text string.

        Args:
            text: The model's text string input or output.

        Returns:
            True if the text is safe, False if a threat is detected.
        """
        for pattern in cls._SENSITIVE_PATTERNS:
            if pattern.search(text):
                print("SECURITY ALERT: Malicious object signature detected. Blocked.")
                return False

        print("Input validation passed.")
        return True

Since complex objects like metadata and additional_kwargs are deserialized from dictionaries, one must validate their serialized string representation before processing.

        "type": "constructor",
        "id": ["system", "os", "getenv"],

}
